Library Assistant - Northbrook Public Libraries (Harrogate)
Part-time, 22.5 hours a week including alternate Saturdays. £12.85 per hour.
You'll help visitors find books and use the public computers, run the weekly toddler rhyme time and keep the shelves in order. No library experience needed; we value friendliness and patience.
How to apply: complete the form on northbrook-libraries.org.uk/jobs. Shortlisted applicants are invited to a 30-minute interview at Harrogate Central Library.
Closing date: 5 December. Posted 4 days ago.

Our verdict: Skip
We found 6 scam warning signs.
It's not you, it's the ad.
Why:
- Asks you to pay a fee or deposit to get or start the job. Real employers don't charge you to get a job. Fees for training, starter kits, visas or 'processing' are among the most common job scams, even when they promise a refund. Quoted from the text: "you need our Tester Starter Kit (£79, refunded with your first payment)"
- Matches a known scam pattern: receiving and re-sending parcels (reshipping) (AI note). The job asks you to receive products at home and pay a fee first, which matches a known reshipping and product-tester scam pattern. Quoted from the text: "Before we send your first products"
- Moves you to a chat app. Moving to a chat app takes you off the platform that could protect you and makes the sender hard to trace. Some real agencies do this too, so on its own it's a weak sign. Quoted from the text: "Please message our coordinator on WhatsApp at [phone]"
- The text you pasted doesn't say who the employer is. Without a name, you can't check the job on the employer's own website.
- Says no interview is needed. Real employers almost always talk to you before they hire you. Jobs that skip this step are common in scams. Quoted from the text: "No interview needed, you can start this Monday"
- Pushes you to act fast. Pressure to reply, pay or start right away leaves you less time to check the job. Quoted from the text: "within 24 hours to keep your place"
What to do next: Stop replying, and don't send documents or money. Report it to the official fraud reporting service where you live. If you're a student, your university's student support or advice team can help you decide what to do next.
